definition: Inductive logic programming (ILP) is a subfield of symbolic artificial intelligence which uses logic programming as a uniform representation for examples, background knowledge and hypotheses.
details: The term "inductive" here refers to philosophical (i.e. suggesting a theory to explain observed facts) rather than mathematical (i.e. proving a property for all members of a well-ordered set) induction. Given an encoding of the known background knowledge and a set of examples represented as a logical database of facts, an ILP system will derive a hypothesised logic program which entails all the positive and none of the negative examples. Schema: positive examples + negative examples + background knowledge ⇒ hypothesis. Bioinformatics and drug design have been highlighted as a principal application area of inductive logic programming techniques.

explainer.lead: Inductive logic programming learns logical rules that explain given examples while ruling out counterexamples, producing hypotheses that are readable as logic programs. It matters where you need learned rules a human can inspect rather than an opaque model.

tiers.eli5: You give the system some things that are true and some that are false, plus what it already knows, and it works out a rule that covers all the true ones and none of the false ones.
tiers.practitioner: Practitioners feed positive examples, negative examples, and background knowledge as logical facts and let the system derive a program that entails positives and excludes negatives. The pitfall is that search over the hypothesis space grows quickly, so scale is a real constraint.
tiers.paperLevel: Given background knowledge B, positive examples E+ and negative examples E-, an ILP system derives a hypothesis H such that B and H together entail every member of E+ and none of E-. The 'inductive' here is philosophical — proposing a theory to explain facts — not mathematical induction.

explainer.example: With facts about family relations, an ILP system could derive a recursive rule for ancestor from examples of who is and is not an ancestor of whom.
